title: How much is it?
title_target: ဘယ်လောက်လဲ — bè-lowk-lè:
goal: Count up to a hundred thousand, read Burmese digits, and ask prices — including the way people in Myanmar talk about money, which is built nothing like English.
bekal: count from one to a hundred in Burmese
read the ten Burmese digits on license plates and price tags
ask the price with ဘယ်လောက်လဲ
give prices in သောင်း and သိန်း
say expensive, cheap, and I have no money

dialogs.title: စကားပြော — At a bookshop near the office
dialogs.intro: Ani is looking for a dictionary. Notice how the shop owner gives prices: he doesn't count the zeros one by one; he uses the unit သောင်း (ten thousand). That's how every price is said in Myanmar, and tourists who aren't used to it almost always fall behind.

grammars.title: Numbers one to ten, then all the rest
body: The first ten numbers must be learned by heart. After that, Burmese is very regular: tens are formed as "how many × ten", and the units are simply tacked on.

head: Number
Burmese
Say it
Note
rows: ဆယ် → ဆယ့် before a digit
နှစ်ဆယ့်ငါး

after: ⚠️ Notice that **တစ်ဆယ့်ခြောက်** (16) is read *ta.hsay.hchowk*: ဆယ် turns into ဆယ့်, with a creaky tone, as soon as another digit follows it. This small change happens in every teen and every two-digit number, so get used to it now.

grammars.title: ⚠️ သောင်း and သိန်း — how Myanmar talks about money
body: English counts money in "thousands" and "millions". Burmese slips two extra units in between, and **almost every price in Myanmar is given in those two units**.

head: Amount
Burmese
Say it
How it's said
rows: တစ်သောင်းငါးထောင်
ဆယ့်ငါးသိန်း

after: The fastest way to get used to it: stop translating and start **thinking in multiples of ten thousand**. A room rent of 150,000 kyat isn't "a hundred and fifty thousand" but ဆယ့်ငါးသိန်း — "fifteen" in units of သိန်း.
The currency is the ကျပ် (*chak*), but in everyday speech the word is often **not said at all**. If someone says ရှစ်ထောင်, they certainly mean eight thousand kyat.

grammars.title: Asking prices and bargaining
body: Bargaining is normal at markets and small stalls, but not in big shops or anywhere with price tags. These sentences cover the whole business.

head: Burmese
Say it
English
rows: ဘယ်လောက်လဲ
ဈေးကြီးတယ်
ပိုက်ဆံ မပါဘူး
I don't have money on me
ဒါ ယူပါ့မယ်

after: ⚠️ ဈေး (*zay:*) means both "price" and "market". ဈေးကြီးတယ် literally means "the price is big", and ဈေးသွားတယ် means "go to the market". The sentence always makes the difference clear.

grammars.title: …လောက် and …ပဲ — about and only
body: Two small words that make price talk sound natural, and both go **after** the number.

head: Burmese
Say it
Meaning
rows: တစ်သောင်းလောက်
ရှစ်ထောင်ပဲ
နည်းနည်းပဲ

after: ဘယ်လောက် itself is actually built from ဘယ် ("which") + လောက် ("about") — literally "about which". Once you see that, it stops feeling like a new word to memorize.

sections.title: Reading Burmese digits in the street

blocks.text: Burmese digits are still used everywhere: license plates, city bus numbers, market price tags, house numbers, and newspaper dates. They're round like the letters, and some of them look like letters — ၀ has the same shape as the letter ဝ, and ၇ looks like ၅. Five minutes of memorizing them will save you a lot of confusion.

head: Written
Read as
Meaning
rows: ဘတ်စ်ကား ၃၆

blocks.title: The drill that sticks fastest
items: Write your own phone number, your date of birth, and your house number in Burmese digits. You already know all three in ordinary digits, so your brain only has to attach the new shapes to familiar content.
Then read them out loud. ⚠️ Burmese digits are read in exactly the same order as ordinary digits — left to right. Nothing is reversed.
